```{r}
#| label: library

options(housepi.footer.warranty = TRUE)
```

Here we load a housepi model template, then associate the definitions needed to run inference and simulations.

# Format of the data

The dataset is a numerical data.frame with one row per household member.
A minimal dataset looks like this^[
This dataset ships with the "test" model, see `?dummy_household` and `?template_test`.]

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">
<div>

```{r}
#| label: dummy-household-data-table
#| echo: false
env <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
utils::data("dummy_household", package = "housepi", envir = env)
knitr::kable(env[["dummy_household"]])
```

</div>
</div>

A column `"id"` with individual identifiers can be provided to keep track of changes and make errors more readable.
Without it, housepi tags individuals with row numbers.

To group individuals in households, a column `"hh_id"` with the respective household tag needs to be present.
Individuals with the same household id will then be considered to belong to the same household.
No household id implies that all individuals in the data are living separately.

To perform model inference, a `"status"` must be provided for each individual $i$.
Status $s_{i}$ should be an integer value satisfying the following convention:

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">
<div>

| Status $s_{i}$ | Compartment | Serology     |
|:--------------:|-------------|--------------|
| $\geq$ `1`     | infectious  | seropositive |
| `0`            | escaped     | seronegative |
| `NA`           | missing     | missing      |

</div>
</div>

In this way we can use the status as a label for different classes of infectious household members.
E.g. we could say that $s_{i} = 1$ refers to symptomatic individuals, and $s_{i} = 2$ to asymptomatic ones.
This is used in advanced latent definitions, see [Data augmentation](data_augmentation.html) for an example.

# The housepi model class

The central element of the package is the [R6 class](https://r6.r-lib.org/articles/Introduction.html) `HousepiModel`.
A dataset can be provided at model construction via the `data` argument of `new_housepi_model()`.
If omitted, it can be attached later with `add_dataset()`.
We generate an instance with the final-size template, on one of the public datasets shipped with housepi, `flu_1918_frederick` (see `?flu_1918_frederick`):

```{r}
#| label: load-model
# import the library
library(housepi)
# specify seed for random number generators
set.seed(42)
# theme for visualizations
set_housepi_theme(colour_strips = TRUE)

# generate an instance of the final-size model with data
hh_model <- new_housepi_model(flu_1918_frederick, "final-size")
```

We can retrieve the template model description by using the method `$help()`.

A brief summary of the loaded data can be obtained via `summarise_house_cases()`,
here manipulated with [flextable](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=flextable):

```{r}
#| label: summarise-house-cases
# show a summary of cases as a `flextable`
summarise_house_cases(hh_model) |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::set_formatter(
    percent = function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", round(x, 1))
  ) |>
  flextable::merge_v(j = ~ level) |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ level + metric, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::labelizor(labels = c(level = "", metric = "", percent = "[%]")) |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

The last row is the count of the equivalence classes, i.e. households that are indistinguishable by the
model (same size, statuses, rates, etc).
The likelihood is then evaluated just once per class, and multiplied by the number of class members.
A sampled latent variable makes every household a class of its own.

At any moment we can re-export the full dataset with `get_dataset()`.

```{r}
#| label: import-data
# data was associated to the model at construction above
head(get_dataset(hh_model))
```

# A collection of models

To see the list of currently available model templates, run

```{r}
#| label: list-templates
# present the list of template model name
browse_templates()
```

Each template comes with definitions that can be used straight away or changed.
To know more about each model, choose a name from the previous list and run, e.g.

```{r}
#| label: model-help
#| eval: false
# open the template help page
browse_templates("final-size")
```

This opens the help page of the template, also reachable with `?template_final_size`.

# Associate parameters

Each parameter needs a definition: the prior and the proposal of the MCMC sampler.
We can call `add_parameter()` as follows:

```{r}
#| label: add-parameters

# single parameter definitions
hh_model <- hh_model |>
  # alpha: baseline community transmission rate
  # name: matching the model requirement
  # prior: uniform with default arguments, min = 0, max = 1
  add_parameter(name = "alpha", prior = "uniform") |>
  # beta: baseline person-to-person transmission rate
  add_parameter("beta", prior = "uniform")

# append parameters using multiple definitions
hh_model <- hh_model |>
  # hh_size_ref: reference household size, constant value
  # gamma: size-scaling of person-to-person rate
  add_parameter(hh_size_ref = 6L, gamma = list(prior = "uniform"))

# inspect parameter definitions
hh_model |> get_parameters()
```

A parameter is defined as constant by passing a value to `const`, as in `add_parameter("gamma", const = 1)`, or as a bare number, as `hh_size_ref` above.
At any moment we can read the parameter definitions of the model by calling `get_parameters()`.

For further information on the available options for priors and MCMC proposals definitions, see [Priors and proposals](priors_and_proposals.html).

# Run inference

Once the definitions are in place, `run_inference()` runs the inference.
With housepi we can perform inference using Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) with the component-wise Metropolis-Hastings algorithm [@metropolis_equation_1953; @hastings_monte_1970].
Standard options for the MCMC can be provided at this stage, including controls on the number of `threads`.
Runs after the same `set.seed()` call draw the same chains whatever the number of `threads`.
The draws come as [posterior](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=posterior) objects that can be accessed to compute estimates.

```{r}
#| label: run-inference
# run the Monte Carlo specifying its settings (equal to default)
hh_fit <- hh_model |>
  run_inference(steps = 2000, # steps per chain, after adaptation
                thin = 10,    # keep one step every ten
                adapt = 1000, # adaptation steps, run before `steps`
                chains = 4,   # independent chains
                threads = 1)  # parallel threads

# report 95% credible intervals (default is 90%, as in `posterior`)
set_housepi_summary(cri_level = 0.95)

# summarise posterior draws of parameters
hh_fit |> summarise_draws()
```

We can extract the parameter draws with `get_parameter_draws()` and plot traces with [bayesplot](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=bayesplot):

```{r}
#| label: param-traces
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for alpha and beta parameters across MCMC iterations with four parallel chains overlaid.
# visualize the traces of every chain with 'bayesplot'
get_parameter_draws(hh_fit) |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace(facet_args = list(ncol = 1))
```

# Models with data augmentation

Models with latent variables are defined in a similar way.
[Data augmentation](data_augmentation.html) covers latent definitions in depth.
Here we present a case study, using the template model "case-ascertained" (see `?template_case_ascertained`) where households are conditioned on a single introduction.
The household structure comes from the `sarscov2_2021_icofs` dataset (see `?sarscov2_2021_icofs`).
We load the parameter definitions directly from the model template.

```{r}
#| label: load-latent-model
# select a data structure (used later for the simulation)
community_structure <- sarscov2_2021_icofs |>
  dplyr::select(id, hh_id)

hh_model <- community_structure |>
  new_housepi_model("case-ascertained") |>
  add_parameter(import = "template") |>
  add_infectivity_profile(import = "template")

# inspect current definitions
hh_model |> get_parameters()
hh_model |> get_infectivity_profiles()
```

In this example we passed `import = "template"` to load the parameter definitions shipped with the transmission model.

# Simulate an outbreak

We define the latent variables with `add_latent()`.
Infection times are generated by the transmission model, which gives their probability: they take no `model`, only the bounds `min` and `max` that inference samples them within.
In simulation, the transmission model sets every infection time, starting from the primary case of each household, infected on day 0.
Incubation periods are not generated by transmission, so they need a `model`.
Alongside latent definitions, we need to define observations, in this case of the symptom onset dates and of the start date derived from them.
We do so with `add_observation()`.

```{r}
#| label: load-latent-definitions
hh_model <- hh_model |>
  add_latent(
    # infection time, generated by the transmission model,
    # sampled in inference within these bounds
    infec_time = list(min = start_date - 14, max = onset_date + 1),
    # incubation period for each individual
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma", mean = 2, sd = 1, max = 14)
  ) |>
  add_observation(
    # observation of onset date noisy around the real onset time
    onset_date = list(discr = TRUE, model = "normal", min = floor(infec_time),
                      mean = infec_time + incub_period),
    # followup starts with earliest onset date (house-level observation)
    start_date = list(func = min(onset_date), level = "house"),
    # followup ends after 3 weeks after first onset
    end_date = start_date + 21
  )
```

Printing the model lists the definitions in place and the ones still missing:

```{r}
#| label: print-model-state
# print current state of definitions
hh_model
```

By default, if no group rate definition is provided all values are set to 1 (reference value).
To see how to associate group rates in heterogeneous models, see [Group rates](group_rates.html).
We can overlook these alerts for the rest of the walkthrough.
The infectivity profile, instead, is mandatory for this model: above we loaded the one shipped with it, and [Infectivity profiles](infectivity_profiles.html) shows how to provide a custom definition.

We run a simulation with the method `run_simulation`, using the same community structure from the study.
The parameter values come as `draws`: a parameter without a value is drawn from its prior.
Each household's outbreak starts from one member drawn at random, its primary case.
Every infected individual gets an incubation period, an infection time and a sampled onset date:

```{r}
#| label: run-simulation
# parameter values of the simulation
sim_values <- c(alpha = 1e-3, beta = 0.15, gamma = 1)

# the onset_date observation is sampled automatically
simulated <- hh_model |> run_simulation(sim_values)

head(simulated)
```

To mimic how the study was reported, such as rounded dates or missed cases, attach functions with `add_reporting_process()`: every simulated study goes through them before it is returned.

# Validation

A simulation study checks that inference recovers the parameters used for the simulation.
We attach the simulated study as data and keep the definitions used to simulate it, so the simulated `onset_date` enters inference as an observation.

```{r}
#| label: inference-simulated

# associate the simulated data to the model
hh_model <- hh_model |>
  add_dataset(simulated)

# run inference on two threads, updating progress bar every 3 seconds
hh_fit <- hh_model |> run_inference(threads = 2, progress = 3)
```

Besides the parameters, the fit holds the pointwise `log_lik`, the per-household complete-data log-likelihood, which includes the latent models.
We plot the traces against the values used for the simulation:

```{r}
#| label: validation-traces
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Trace plots for alpha, beta, and gamma parameters with four chains.
#|  Overlaying orange lines indicate the values used for the simulation.
library(ggplot2)

# extract sample to posterior draws_df
param_draws <- get_parameter_draws(hh_fit)

# original parameters used for the simulation
simul_parameters <- data.frame(parameter = names(sim_values),
                               simulated = sim_values)

# use bayesplot to plot the posterior draws
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(param_draws, facet_args = list(ncol = 1)) +
  geom_hline(data = simul_parameters, aes(yintercept = simulated))
```

The R-hat diagnostics [@vehtari_rank_normalization_2021] check that the chains converged:

```{r}
#| label: rhat-diagnostics
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-alt: >
#|  R-hat convergence diagnostics for alpha, beta, and gamma parameters with color-coded thresholds.
#|  Color intensity represents R-hat values (≤1.05, ≤1.1, >1.1). Points near 1.0 indicate convergence.
# compute Rhat values associated to inferred parameters
var_names <- get_parameters(hh_model) |>
  dplyr::filter(is.na(const)) |>
  dplyr::pull(name)
rhat_table <- summarise_draws(param_draws, rhat = posterior::rhat)
rhat_values <- setNames(rhat_table$rhat, rhat_table$variable)[var_names]

# use bayesplot to showcase Rhat statistics
bayesplot::mcmc_rhat(rhat_values) +
  bayesplot::yaxis_text(hjust = 1)
```

The table puts the estimates next to the values used for the simulation.

```{r}
#| label: parameter-comparison-table
param_draws |>
  summarise_draws() |>
  format_estimates() |>
  dplyr::select(parameter = variable, inferred = formatted) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(simul_parameters, by = "parameter") |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::separate_header() |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ parameter, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

A single simulated study can miss the truth by chance: [performance checks](performance_checks.html) repeat it many times.
Alongside them, [posterior predictive checks](predictive_checks.html) can be used to compare observed household measures against model posterior predicted measures.
